ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

forearm shaft — clinical pattern 1

An adult has a displaced fracture of the distal third of the radial shaft after a fall. The wrist is painful, and dedicated films show distal radioulnar joint incongruity with displacement of the ulnar head. The proximal radial head remains located. Which injury pattern is present?

  1. Monteggia fracture-dislocation
  2. Essex-Lopresti injury
  3. Isolated ulnar shaft fracture
  4. Both-bone forearm shaft fracture
  5. Galeazzi fracture-dislocation
Answer and explanation

Galeazzi fracture-dislocation

A radial shaft fracture is associated with disruption of the distal radioulnar joint.

Option explanations

Galeazzi fracture-dislocation: A radial shaft fracture is associated with disruption of the distal radioulnar joint.

Monteggia fracture-dislocation: An ulnar fracture or deformity is accompanied by radial head dislocation. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Essex-Lopresti injury: A radial head fracture is associated with interosseous membrane disruption and distal radioulnar joint injury. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Isolated ulnar shaft fracture: A direct blow may fracture the ulnar shaft without radial fracture or associated proximal or distal joint disruption. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Both-bone forearm shaft fracture: Fractures of both radial and ulnar shafts can disrupt the alignment required for pronation and supination. This is not the pattern specified in this case.
